title: The Morning Brief: Courts block Trump moves; primary races take shape
dek: A federal judge halted the Trump administration's plan to relocate FBI headquarters from Maryland to Washington, while two primary elections clarified November matchups in Florida and Alaska. Meanwhile, legal challenges mounted against the administration and Trump himself on multiple fronts.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: The morning shows courts constraining executive action on infrastructure and regulatory matters, while ballot outcomes in two states narrowed the field for consequential fall races.
bottom_line: Monday's rulings constrained executive action on the FBI relocation and left regulatory retribution claims pending before a federal judge, while primary outcomes in Florida and Alaska narrowed general election fields. Watch for the Trump administration's response to the Maryland ruling, whether it appeals or seeks congressional action, and for the federal judge's decision on Disney's request for a temporary restraining order in the broadcast licensing dispute. The federal investigation into the Alaska Senate race candidate bears monitoring as ranked-choice voting approaches.
body: A federal judge on Monday blocked the Trump administration from scrapping the FBI headquarters relocation to Greenbelt, Maryland. U.S. District Judge Theodore D. Chuang, an appointee of President Barack Obama, ruled that the administration's attempt to move the facility to the Ronald Reagan Building in Washington exceeded statutory authority and was not in accordance with law. The decision prevents the administration from redirecting funds Congress had allocated to the Maryland project and protects Maryland and Prince George's County's decade-long investment and hundreds of millions of dollars in pledges to secure the headquarters.

Two separate legal actions challenged Trump administration positions. Disney and ABC filed suit on August 18, 2026, against the Federal Communications Commission, alleging a retaliatory regulatory campaign over broadcast content. The lawsuit seeks to block an order requiring eight Disney-owned ABC television stations to file license renewal applications years ahead of schedule, with only thirty days to prepare filings that ordinarily take months. Disney's legal team, which includes prominent attorneys Beth Wilkinson and Paul Clement, called the directive unprecedented and characterized it as an existential threat. The FCC disputes the retaliation claim, citing ongoing investigations into Disney's diversity practices and "The View" program's compliance with public interest standards. Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison filed a federal lawsuit against Texas Governor Greg Abbott to compel the extradition of ICE agent Christian Castro, who faces charges of assault with a deadly weapon and falsely reporting a crime in connection with allegedly shooting a Venezuelan man in Minneapolis on January 14.

In a third legal matter affecting Trump, the Supreme Court declined to reconsider its June rejection of his appeal challenging a $5 million jury verdict in an E. Jean Carroll defamation case. The Court did not explain its action and there were no noted dissents. Rehearing requests are almost never granted; no such request has been approved since the 1960s. Trump has already paid the judgment plus interest, with Carroll's representatives confirming receipt in July. A separate $83.3 million verdict in another Carroll case remains under review at the Court.

On the campaign front, primary elections advanced two consequential November matchups. Rep. Byron Donalds won the Republican primary for Florida governor while former Rep. David Jolly won the Democratic primary, setting up a contest to succeed term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis. Donalds, backed by President Trump and a prominent House Freedom Caucus member, faces a state that has shifted significantly rightward. In Alaska's U.S. Senate race, GOP incumbent Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola both advanced to the November general election, which will be decided by ranked-choice voting. A third candidate, Dan J. Sullivan, a former teacher running as a Republican, is the subject of a federal grand jury investigation into whether his candidacy is part of a conspiracy to confuse voters. NBC News reports that the grand jury issued subpoenas last week to compel information from witnesses related to that campaign.

In a separate matter unrelated to federal action, Camron Harris, 19, charged in a Virginia State University shooting that wounded five people on Saturday near Petersburg, sent Instagram messages saying "I'm tryna find the gun" and "We js got the shootin," according to court documents. The early-morning attack on the historically Black university critically injured a 21-year-old man and wounded four others with non-life-threatening injuries. Harris faces multiple felony charges and remains in custody.
